content: This review is an update of a previously published analysis in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Refractory status epilepticus (RSE) is a condition where seizures persist despite the use of antiepileptic drugs. In such cases, anesthetic drugs are often used to induce a coma to achieve complete seizure control. Among these, thiopental sodium and propofol are commonly employed. Both drugs have demonstrated effectiveness, but there is insufficient evidence to determine which is superior in terms of clinical outcomes. The objective of this review was to compare the efficacy, adverse effects, and both shortand long-term outcomes of RSE treatment using either thiopental sodium or propofol. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, and ClinicalTrials.gov, among others, up to August 16, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving patients of any age or gender were included if they assessed the control of RSE using either of these two anesthetic agents. Two authors independently screened the search results and reviewed abstracts of eligible studies before retrieving full-text publications. Only one study, involving 24 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This was a small, single-blind, multicenter trial that investigated adults with RSE treated with either propofol or thiopental sodium. However, the study was terminated prematurely due to recruitment challenges. For the primary outcome of complete seizure control after the first course of the study drug, 6 out of 14 patients in the propofol group achieved control compared to 2 out of 7 patients in the thiopental sodium group. The calculated risk ratio (RR) was 1.50, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.40 to 5.61, indicating low-quality evidence. Mortality was observed in 3 out of 14 patients in the propofol group and 1 out of 7 patients in the thiopental sodium group (RR 1.50, 95% CI 0.19 to 11.93, also low-quality evidence). The length of ICU stay was not reported in this study. Regarding secondary outcomes, adverse events such as infections occurred in 7 out of 14 patients in the propofol group and 5 out of 7 patients in the thiopental sodium group (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.41). Hypotension requiring vasopressor support was noted in 7 out of 14 patients in the propofol group and 4 out of 7 patients in the thiopental sodium group (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.38 to 2.00). A severe but non-fatal complication, propofol infusion syndrome, was reported in one patient. Patients treated with thiopental sodium required a longer duration of mechanical ventilation compared to those treated with propofol, with a median of 17 days (range: 5 to 70 days) versus 4 days (range: 2 to 28 days), respectively. At the three-month follow-up, there was no significant difference between the two drugs in terms of seizure control or functional outcomes. The authors concluded that there is still a lack of robust, randomized, controlled evidence to determine the relative efficacy of propofol and thiopental sodium in the treatment of RSE. Large-scale RCTs are urgently needed to address this critical clinical question.
